title: The icon corner
hook: Orthodox homes keep a beautiful corner for prayer

segments.voice: Yesterday, bedtime prayers, the short ones learned young and sometimes kept for life. Your line was keep me through the night. Did any old words come back as you lay down? Day one thousand three hundred seventy-two.

Up near the ceiling, in the corner of a living room, there's a small shelf. On it stand a few painted faces on wood: Christ, his mother, a saint or two. A little oil lamp flickers in red glass. A dried palm branch is tucked behind one frame. On the other wall, the television. On the table, homework and a set of keys. Nobody here built a chapel. They gave one corner of an ordinary room a different job. Some Orthodox families stand in front of a shelf like this to pray in the morning and again at night. Today: the icon corner.
screen: `FACES ON WOOD, A LAMP IN RED GLASS.`

segments.voice: Start with the name. In Russian homes it has been called the beautiful corner, and other Orthodox families keep their own versions. Tradition puts it on the east wall where the room allows, toward the sunrise. Icons of Christ and Mary sit there, often with the saints the family are named for. It's small on purpose: a shelf, not a shrine room. Next, why a place at all. Jesus, in the Sermon on the Mount, in the King James Bible: "But thou, when thou prayest, enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret." A closet there means an inner room. Jesus is warning against prayer put on for an audience. A corner in your own home fits that: nobody is watching but the faces on the shelf. Then, the habit. In the book of Daniel, a new law forbids prayer to anyone but the king, and Daniel goes home anyway. "His windows being open in his chamber toward Jerusalem, he kneeled upon his knees three times a day, and prayed, and gave thanks before his God, as he did aforetime." A room. A direction. A time. As he did aforetime: the habit was there before the trouble came. Last, why heaven. Jacob, running from his brother, sleeps outdoors and dreams of a ladder reaching to heaven. He wakes and says, "Surely the LORD is in this place; and I knew it not." And then: "this is none other but the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven." The icon corner says the same thing about a living room. Other Christians keep their own versions: a Catholic home altar with a crucifix and a statue of Mary, or a chair by the window with a worn Bible on the arm. The shape changes. The idea holds: one spot kept for remembering Jacob's words, the LORD is in this place.

Here's the practice: make a small prayer corner. Settle, and breathe. Look around wherever you are and choose one spot: a shelf, a windowsill, the corner of a desk, the top of a dresser. In your mind, clear it. Then choose one thing to set there. A cross. An icon or a holy picture. A candle. A Bible. A photo of someone you want to remember. Just one. Picture it in its place, and picture sitting in front of it tomorrow morning. If you pray, you can pray there in your own words or your church's, the way Daniel kept his window. If you don't, let it be a corner kept for quiet. The bell holds the time.
The icon corner. A small place at home set apart for prayer, with icons, a lamp, and the things a family holds holy.
Your line: a corner of heaven. Today, actually set up the spot you chose, even with one object, and stop there once before bed. Day one thousand three hundred seventy-two.

howItsDone: Some Orthodox Christians keep an icon corner at home, with icons, a lamp and a prayer book, and pray there in the morning and evening; some Catholic families keep a home altar, and other Christians keep a quiet chair or shelf for prayer.

original.note: Greek: an inner room or storeroom, the word behind "closet" in Matthew 6:6.

what a scholar hears: tameion, the inner room of Matthew 6:6, and Jacob at Bethel: none other but the house of God, and the gate of heaven.

notes: 'Beautiful corner' (Russian krasny ugol) is taken from the index hook; confirm the naming and that 'other Orthodox families keep their own versions' is fair.
'Tradition puts it on the east wall where the room allows': confirm.
Hook scene (red lamp, palm branch, morning and evening prayer) is a composite illustration; confirm it is typical and fairly described.
Catholic home altar and the Protestant-style 'chair by the window with a Bible' are offered as parallels without ranking; confirm.
Original: ταμεῖον (also spelled ταμιεῖον) as inner room/storeroom in Matthew 6:6; confirm spelling and gloss.
Daniel 6:10 quoted from 'his windows'; the verse reads 'and his windows being open'. Confirm.
Editor pass: the teach's last line no longer has the narrator assert that God is in the place; it now points back to Jacob's words.
Audit (fresh reviewer): checked all KJV quotations (Matt 6:6, Dan 6:10, Gen 28:16–17) against the 1769 text; no changes needed.
